subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on chemical bonding and structure, then mark my answer against the CCEA spec.
promptWeak: Explain chemical bonding and structure for GCSE CCEA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Ionic bonding is best described as:
options: Shared pairs of electrons between atoms
Attraction between fixed positive ions and delocalised electrons
The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
questions.explain: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions (formed by transfer of electrons).

questions.q: A positively charged ion is called a:
questions.explain: A cation is a positive ion (formed by losing electrons). An anion is a negative ion (formed by gaining electrons).

questions.q: When sodium (2,8,1) forms an ion, what happens?
options: It loses 1 electron to form Na+
It gains 7 electrons to form Na7-
It gains 1 electron to form Na-
questions.explain: Sodium has 1 outer electron. It loses this electron to form Na+ with a full outer shell (2,8).

questions.q: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed between magnesium (Mg2+) and chloride (Cl-)?
questions.explain: Charges must balance: one Mg2+ needs two Cl- ions to give a neutral compound, so MgCl2.

questions.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
options: They are made of small molecules
Strong electrostatic forces throughout the giant ionic lattice need a lot of energy to break
questions.explain: Ionic compounds form a giant lattice with strong electrostatic forces in all directions, requiring lots of energy (high temperature) to overcome.
When molten or in solution the ions are free to move and carry charge. In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice.

questions.q: A covalent bond is formed when:
options: Electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal
A pair of electrons is shared between two atoms
questions.explain: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two (usually non-metal) atoms.

questions.q: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom form in methane (CH4)?
questions.explain: Carbon has 4 outer electrons and forms 4 single covalent bonds, one to each hydrogen atom.

questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances such as water have low melting and boiling points?
options: The weak intermolecular forces between molecules are easily overcome
questions.explain: The covalent bonds within molecules are strong, but the intermolecular forces between separate molecules are weak and need little energy to overcome.

questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances not conduct electricity?
options: They have no charged particles free to move
questions.explain: Molecules are neutral overall with no free ions or delocalised electrons, so there are no charge carriers.

questions.q: Which of these is a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure?
questions.explain: Diamond is a giant covalent structure of carbon atoms. Carbon dioxide and oxygen are simple molecules; sodium chloride is ionic.

questions.q: Why do giant covalent structures like diamond have very high melting points?
options: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken
questions.explain: A large amount of energy is needed to break the many strong covalent bonds throughout the giant lattice.

questions.q: Why can graphite conduct electricity while diamond cannot?
options: Each carbon in graphite bonds to only 3 others, leaving delocalised electrons free to move
questions.explain: In graphite each carbon forms 3 covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move and carry charge. In diamond all 4 outer electrons are in bonds.

questions.q: Why is graphite slippery and used as a lubricant?
options: It is made of layers held together by weak forces that can slide over each other
questions.explain: Graphite has layers of carbon atoms; the weak forces between layers allow them to slide, making it soft and slippery.

questions.q: Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between:
options: Fixed positive ions and a sea of delocalised electrons
questions.explain: In a metal, positive ions are arranged in a lattice surrounded by delocalised electrons; the attraction between them is metallic bonding.

options: They have ions free to move
They contain delocalised electrons that are free to move and carry charge
questions.explain: The delocalised (free) electrons in a metal can move through the structure, carrying an electric charge.

questions.q: Why are metals malleable (can be hammered into shape)?
options: Layers of positive ions can slide over each other while metallic bonding is maintained
questions.explain: Layers of metal ions slide over one another without breaking the metallic bond, so the metal changes shape without shattering.

questions.q: Why is an alloy usually harder than the pure metal?
options: Different sized atoms distort the regular layers so they cannot slide over each other easily
questions.explain: In an alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular arrangement, making it harder for layers to slide, so the alloy is harder.

questions.q: A substance has a high melting point, does not conduct as a solid, but conducts when molten. What is its structure?
questions.explain: These are classic properties of an ionic compound: high melting point (strong lattice) and conduction only when ions are free to move (molten or dissolved).
